topics.name: Standard deviation
topics.kicker: How spread out data are · The square root of the variance
topics.dates: Named in print by Karl Pearson, 1894
topics.briefing: Standard deviation measures how spread out a set of numbers is: small when the data huddle close to the average, and large when they scatter far away. To find it, you average the squared distances from the mean (that average is called the variance) and then take the square root. On a bell curve, about 68% of the data lie within one standard deviation of the mean, and about 95% lie within two.
topics.answerHtml: standard deviation (accept SD; prompt on sigma or deviation; do not accept “variance”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Pafnuty Chebyshev’s [“cheh-bih-SHOFFS”] inequality guarantees that, for any data set at all, at least three-quarters of the values lie within two of these quantities of the mean, and at least eight-ninths lie within three of them. This quantity is the root-mean-square distance of data values from their mean.
tossups.r: For a bell curve, about 68 percent of values lie within one of these of the mean. For 10 points, name this measure of spread, the square root of the variance.

tossups.p: Bessel’s correction divides by n minus 1 instead of n when this quantity is estimated from a sample, because a sample’s values sit a little closer to their own average than to the true mean. That sample version of this statistic is usually written with the letter s.
tossups.r: The population version is written with the lowercase Greek letter sigma. For 10 points, name this measure of how spread out data are.

tossups.p: The two inflection points of a bell curve, where it switches from curving downward to curving upward, lie exactly this far on either side of the center. The formula for that curve’s height has this quantity times the square root of 2 pi in its denominator.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this measure of spread, symbolized by sigma, whose square is the variance.

tossups.p: A quality-control method begun at Motorola in the 1980s aims for no more than 3.4 defects per million chances, and its name combines the number six with this quantity’s symbol. Most IQ tests are scaled so that the mean is 100 and this quantity is 15.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this measure of spread, the square root of the variance, written with a lowercase sigma.

tossups.p: Physicists at CERN announced the Higgs boson in 2012 after their signal reached five of these units away from what chance alone would produce. A z-score counts how many of these units a value lies above or below the mean.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this measure of how spread out a data set is, the square root of the variance.

tossups.p: The coefficient of variation divides this quantity by the mean, so that the spread of elephant weights and mouse weights can be compared fairly. Unlike the variance, which has squared units, this quantity has the same units as the data themselves.
tossups.r: In a bell curve, about 68 percent of the data fall within one of these of the mean. For 10 points, name this measure of spread.

tossups.p: Pearson’s correlation coefficient divides the covariance of two variables by the product of their values of this quantity, which keeps the result between negative 1 and 1. Adding the same number to every value in a data set does not change this quantity.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this statistic, the square root of the variance, which measures how spread out data are.

tossups.p: Investors measure the volatility of a stock by finding this quantity for its returns, and Bollinger bands on stock charts are usually drawn two of these units above and below a moving average of the price. Error bars on graphs often reach this far above and below each average.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this measure of spread, symbolized by a lowercase sigma, whose square is the variance.

tossups.p: When independent measurements are added together, their variances add, but this quantity does not; instead, it combines like the sides of a right triangle, as the square root of a sum of squares. Independent errors of 3 and 4 units therefore combine to give 5.
tossups.r: This quantity is symbolized by a lowercase sigma. For 10 points, name this measure of spread, the square root of the variance.

tossups.p: The Cauchy [“koh-SHEE”] distribution, which looks like a bell curve with fatter tails, has no defined mean or variance, so this quantity does not exist for it. A normal distribution, by contrast, is completely described by its mean and this quantity.
tossups.r: About 95 percent of a bell curve lies within two of these of the mean. For 10 points, name this measure of spread.

tossups.p: For a single roll of a fair six-sided die, this quantity is about 1.71. For the number of heads in 100 fair coin flips, the average is 50 heads and this quantity is exactly 5. This quantity is 0 only when every value is the same.
tossups.r: Squaring it gives the variance, which is 25 for those coin flips. For 10 points, name this measure of spread.

tossups.p: The eight values 2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 7, and 9 have a mean of 5, and their squared distances from that mean average out to 4, which makes this statistic equal to 2. Unlike the range, which uses only the largest and smallest values, this statistic depends on every value.
tossups.r: This statistic has the same units as the data. For 10 points, name this measure of spread, symbolized sigma, whose square is the variance.

tossups.p: Karl Pearson first used this statistic’s name in print in 1894, and in 1918 Ronald Fisher coined a name for the square of this statistic in a paper about how traits are inherited. A z-score divides a value’s distance from the mean by this statistic.
tossups.r: Fisher’s name for its square, variance, also appears in his technique ANOVA. For 10 points, name this square root of the variance.

tossups.p: A shortcut formula finds the square of this statistic by taking the mean of the squares of the values and subtracting the square of the mean. For the data 1, 2, and 3, that gives 14 thirds minus 4, or two-thirds.
tossups.r: Dividing this statistic by the square root of the sample size gives the standard error. For 10 points, name this square root of the variance, symbolized sigma.

tossups.p: Because it squares each distance from the mean, this statistic is never smaller than the average absolute distance from the mean, and it is pulled upward more strongly by outliers. Multiplying every value in a data set by 10 multiplies this statistic by 10 as well.
tossups.r: On a bell curve, about 99.7 percent of the data lie within three of these of the mean. For 10 points, name this measure of spread.

clues.t: Measures how spread out a data set is around its mean (average)
The square root of the variance, so the variance is its square
Written with the lowercase Greek letter sigma (σ) for a whole population, or the letter s for a sample
68–95–99.7 rule: on a bell curve, about 68%, 95%, and 99.7% of the data lie within 1, 2, and 3 of these of the mean
Average the squared distances from the mean, then take the square root (a “root-mean-square”); unlike the range, it uses every value
The data 2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 7, 9 have mean 5, squared distances that average 4, and a value of 2 for it
Has the same units as the data, while the variance has squared units
It is 0 only when every value is the same; adding a constant to every value leaves it unchanged; multiplying every value by 10 multiplies it by 10
A z-score counts how many of these a value lies above or below the mean (distance from the mean divided by it)
Most IQ tests are scaled to a mean of 100 and a value of 15 for it
Error bars on graphs often reach this far above and below each average
Dividing it by the square root of the sample size gives the standard error of a sample mean
Chebyshev’s inequality: for any data set, at least 3/4 of the values lie within 2 of these of the mean, and at least 8/9 within 3
Bessel’s correction: for a sample, divide by n − 1 instead of n, because sample values sit closer to their own average than to the true mean
A bell curve’s two inflection points lie exactly this far from its center; its height formula has this times √(2π) in the denominator
Six Sigma, a quality-control method begun at Motorola in the 1980s, aims for 3.4 defects per million and is named for its symbol
Physicists at CERN announced the Higgs boson in 2012 after their signal reached five of these (“five sigma”) from what chance alone would give
The coefficient of variation divides it by the mean, so the spreads of very different things can be compared
Pearson’s correlation coefficient divides the covariance by the product of two of these, keeping the result between −1 and 1
Investors call it the volatility of a stock’s returns; Bollinger bands are drawn 2 of these above and below a moving average
For independent quantities, variances add but these do not: errors of 3 and 4 combine to 5, like the sides of a right triangle
The Cauchy distribution has no defined mean or variance, so it has none of this either; a normal curve is fixed by its mean and this
For a fair die roll it is about 1.71 (variance 35/12); for heads in 100 fair coin flips it is exactly 5 (variance 25)
Shortcut formula: its square equals the mean of the squares minus the square of the mean (for 1, 2, 3: 14/3 − 4 = 2/3)
Karl Pearson first used its name in print in 1894; Ronald Fisher named its square the “variance” in 1918 and built ANOVA (analysis of variance)
Because it squares distances, it is never smaller than the average absolute distance from the mean and is pulled up more by outliers

trap.title: Variance or its square root?
trap.body: Standard deviation and variance are separate answer lines. The variance is the average squared distance from the mean, and the standard deviation is its square root. A tossup that says “the square of this quantity is the variance” wants standard deviation, but one that says “the square root of this quantity is the standard deviation” wants variance, and real answer lines say “do not accept” the other one. Saying only “sigma” earns a prompt.
trap.fix: Listen for “square” versus “square root,” and for units: standard deviation has the same units as the data, while variance has squared units. If the clue says Ronald Fisher named this quantity itself in 1918, or calls it the thing analyzed in ANOVA, answer “variance.” Mean absolute deviation and standard error are different answer lines too.
trap.line: Real answer line: standard deviation (accept SD; prompt on sigma or deviation; do not accept “variance”)

topics.name: Augustin-Louis Cauchy
topics.kicker: French pioneer of rigorous calculus · Names sequences, inequalities, and more
topics.briefing: Augustin-Louis Cauchy [“koh-SHEE”] was born in Paris in 1789, just weeks after the French Revolution began, and grew into one of the most prolific mathematicians ever, writing about 800 research papers. He made calculus rigorous by carefully defining limits and continuity, and his name is attached to so many ideas, from Cauchy sequences to the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality, that students meet him all over math. His name is one of 72 engraved on the Eiffel Tower.

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In 1810, this man took a job as an engineer building port facilities at Cherbourg [“shair-BOOR”] for the fleet Napoleon planned to send against England. He later wrote _Cours d’analyse_ [“KOOR dah-nah-LEEZ”], a textbook that gave careful definitions of limits and continuity.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this French mathematician whose name is given to sequences whose terms get closer and closer to each other.

tossups.p: After the Bourbon kings returned to power, this man was appointed in 1816 to the Academy of Sciences seat taken from Gaspard Monge [“MOHNZH”], who had been expelled for political reasons. Around that time, this man also won the Academy’s grand prize for a study of waves on the surface of a liquid.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this French mathematician who names an inequality with Hermann Schwarz and a pair of equations with Bernhard Riemann.

tossups.p: After the July Revolution of 1830, this devout royalist refused to swear an oath to King Louis-Philippe and left France, eventually moving to Prague to tutor the grandson of the exiled King Charles X. He did not return to Paris until 1838.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this French mathematician who shares a pair of equations in complex analysis with Bernhard Riemann.

tossups.p: This man was asked to review a long paper that Niels Henrik Abel [“AH-bel”] submitted to the Paris Academy in 1826, but he set it aside and mislaid it, and it was not published until years after Abel’s death. This man wrote about 800 research papers.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this French mathematician whose name is given to an inequality with Hermann Schwarz.

tossups.p: A theorem about when partial differential equations have solutions is named for this man and Sofia Kovalevskaya [“koh-vuh-LYEF-skuh-yuh”], the first woman to earn a modern doctorate in mathematics. This man also developed the calculus of residues for computing difficult integrals in complex analysis.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this French mathematician whose name is given to sequences whose terms get closer and closer together.

tossups.p: In 1813, this man proved that a convex polyhedron whose faces are rigid plates cannot be flexed into a different shape. This man’s name is one of 72 engraved on the Eiffel Tower, along with those of Joseph-Louis Lagrange and Pierre-Simon Laplace.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this French mathematician who shares a pair of equations in complex analysis with Bernhard Riemann.

tossups.p: This man introduced the stress tensor, which describes the forces acting inside a solid or fluid, and helped found the mathematical theory of elasticity. His equation relating a material’s refractive index to the wavelength of light describes how glass spreads white light into colors.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this French mathematician whose name is given to an inequality with Hermann Schwarz and to sequences whose terms bunch closer and closer together.

tossups.p: This man’s extended mean value theorem, which compares the rates of change of two quantities at once, is the key step in the usual proof of L’Hôpital’s [“loh-pee-TAHLZ”] rule for limits. He taught at the École Polytechnique [“ay-KOHL po-leek-tek-NEEK”], where his 1821 textbook made calculus more rigorous.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this French mathematician whose name is given to sequences whose terms get closer and closer together.

tossups.p: This man’s root test and condensation test check whether an infinite series converges, and he shares a formula for a power series’s radius of convergence with Jacques Hadamard [“ah-dah-MAR”]. A bell-shaped probability distribution named for him has such fat tails that it has no defined mean or variance.
tossups.r: Born in Paris in 1789, he names an inequality with Hermann Schwarz. For 10 points, name this French mathematician.

tossups.p: As a boy, this man met Joseph-Louis Lagrange [“luh-GRAHNZH”], who reportedly advised his father to give him a strong education in languages before he studied serious mathematics. He went on to study at the École Polytechnique and then trained as a civil engineer.
tossups.r: This man was born in Paris weeks after the storming of the Bastille in 1789. For 10 points, name this French mathematician who names sequences whose terms get closer and closer together.

tossups.p: This man names the functional equation f of x plus y equals f of x plus f of y, whose only continuous solutions are straight lines through the origin. His integral theorem says that integrating a complex-differentiable function around a closed loop with no holes inside gives zero.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this French mathematician who shares a pair of equations in complex analysis with Bernhard Riemann.

tossups.p: In 1813, this man proved Pierre de Fermat’s claim that every positive whole number is a sum of at most three triangular numbers, four squares, five pentagonal numbers, and so on. Earlier, Joseph-Louis Lagrange had proved the case of squares, and Carl Friedrich Gauss the case of triangular numbers.
tossups.r: His name is one of 72 engraved on the Eiffel Tower. For 10 points, name this French mathematician who names an inequality with Hermann Schwarz.

tossups.p: Carl Friedrich Gauss used the word “determinant” in 1801 for a number tied to quadratic forms, but this man gave the word its modern meaning in 1812. This man also studied how permutations, or rearrangements, can be combined, work that helped launch group theory.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this French mathematician whose name is given to sequences whose terms get closer and closer together.

tossups.p: A theorem named for this man, proved in 1845, says that if a prime number p divides the number of elements in a finite group, then the group contains an element of order p. This man’s rigorous 1821 textbook was called _Cours d’analyse_ [“KOOR dah-nah-LEEZ”].
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this French mathematician who shares a pair of equations in complex analysis with Bernhard Riemann.

tossups.p: This man’s integral formula shows that the values of a complex-differentiable function inside a circle are completely determined by its values on the circle itself. A devout royalist, he refused to swear loyalty to King Louis-Philippe after the revolution of 1830.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this French mathematician who names an inequality with Hermann Schwarz and sequences whose terms get closer and closer together.

trap.title: Which name in the pair?
trap.body: Many of Cauchy’s results share a hyphen with someone else: the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality, the Cauchy–Riemann equations, the Cauchy–Kovalevskaya theorem, and the Cauchy–Hadamard formula. When a tossup says a result is named for “this man and Bernhard Riemann,” the answer is the other name, Cauchy. Other French mathematicians of his time, like Lagrange, Laplace, Fourier, and Galois, show up in the same clues, so a fast buzz on “French mathematician” alone is risky.
trap.fix: Cauchy clues: rigor in calculus (_Cours d’analyse_, 1821), sequences whose terms bunch together, complex integrals around closed loops, exile as a royalist after 1830, and the 72 names on the Eiffel Tower. Galois clues: a duel at age 20 and using groups to study polynomial equations. Fourier clues: heat flow and Fourier series.

topics.name: Group theory
topics.kicker: The math of symmetry · Rubik’s Cubes, crystals, and particles
topics.briefing: Group theory is the math of symmetry. A group is a set of moves, like the turns of a Rubik’s Cube or the rotations and flips of a square, that can be combined and undone, where combining two moves always gives another move in the set. The young French genius Évariste Galois [“gal-WAH”] named groups around 1830 to explain why some equations have no formula for their solutions, and physicists and chemists use groups to sort particles, crystals, and molecules.

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: The largest of the 26 “sporadic” simple examples of these structures, nicknamed the Monster, has about 8 times 10 to the 53rd power elements. In 1998, Richard Borcherds [“BOR-cherdz”] won a Fields Medal partly for proving the “monstrous moonshine” conjecture, which links the Monster to number theory.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these algebraic structures, each a set with an operation that has closure, associativity, an identity, and inverses.

tossups.p: Ludwig Sylow’s [“SEE-lovz”] theorems of 1872 describe the pieces with prime-power sizes inside finite examples of these structures. By Lagrange’s theorem, the size of any smaller one of these sitting inside a finite one must divide the size of the larger one.
tossups.r: The moves of a Rubik’s Cube form one of these. For 10 points, name these algebraic structures that describe symmetry.

tossups.p: Emmy Noether [“NUR-tuh”] proved that every continuous change that leaves the laws of physics the same, such as running an experiment at a later time, comes with a conservation law, such as conservation of energy. Sophus Lie [“LEE”] studied continuous examples of these structures, like the collection of all rotations of a sphere.
tossups.r: The rotations and flips of a square form one of these with 8 elements. For 10 points, name these algebraic structures, which mathematicians use to describe symmetry.

tossups.p: Murray Gell-Mann’s “Eightfold Way” sorted subatomic particles into families using one of these structures called SU(3). The Standard Model of particle physics is built on a combination of three such structures, SU(3), SU(2), and U(1). Gell-Mann won the 1969 Nobel Prize in Physics for classifying particles.
tossups.r: The turns of a Rubik’s Cube form one of these. For 10 points, name these algebraic structures that describe symmetry.

tossups.p: Crystallographers sort the ways a pattern of atoms can repeat in three dimensions into exactly 230 types, and the ways a flat wallpaper pattern can repeat into exactly 17 types. Each of those types is one of these structures.
tossups.r: Évariste Galois [“gal-WAH”] named these structures around 1830. For 10 points, name these algebraic structures, each a set with an associative operation, an identity, and inverses.

tossups.p: Chemists label the shape of a water molecule C2v and the shape of methane Td, using a system in which each label names one of these structures. Chemists use “character tables” for these structures to predict which vibrations of a molecule absorb infrared light.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these mathematical structures that describe symmetry, such as the moves of a Rubik’s Cube.

tossups.p: A theorem named for Augustin-Louis Cauchy [“koh-SHEE”] says that if a prime number p divides the number of elements in a finite one of these structures, then it contains an element that first returns to the identity after exactly p steps. Commutative examples are called abelian, after the Norwegian mathematician Niels Henrik Abel.
tossups.r: The rotations and flips of any shape form one of these. For 10 points, name these algebraic structures, whose four rules are closure, associativity, identity, and inverses.

tossups.p: Felix Klein’s Erlangen [“AIR-lahng-en”] program of 1872 classified geometries by the transformations that leave them unchanged. Klein also names the smallest of these structures that is not cyclic, which has just four elements, each of which is its own inverse.
tossups.r: Clock arithmetic, which adds hours on a 12-hour clock, forms a cyclic one of these. For 10 points, name these structures that describe symmetry.

tossups.p: In 1846, Joseph Liouville [“lee-oo-VEEL”] published the papers of a young Frenchman who had used these structures to study equations, fourteen years after that man died following a duel at age 20. The night before the duel, that man wrote out his ideas in a famous letter to a friend.
tossups.r: That man, Évariste Galois [“gal-WAH”], used them to explain which polynomial equations can be solved with radicals. For 10 points, name these algebraic structures.

tossups.p: Arthur Cayley gave the first abstract definition of these structures in 1854, and his namesake theorem says that every one of them behaves like a collection of rearrangements, or permutations. A Cayley table shows how every pair of elements combines, like a multiplication table.
tossups.r: The integers under addition form one. For 10 points, name these algebraic structures, which must satisfy closure, associativity, identity, and inverses.

tossups.p: William Rowan Hamilton carved the rule i squared equals j squared equals k squared equals ijk equals negative 1 into a Dublin bridge in 1843, and the eight units plus or minus 1, i, j, and k form a non-commutative example of these structures.
tossups.r: Commutative ones are called abelian. For 10 points, name these algebraic structures, studied by Évariste Galois, that describe symmetry.

tossups.p: A proof that every finite simple example of these structures belongs to several infinite families or to a list of 26 exceptions fills tens of thousands of pages written by about 100 authors. The largest exception, the Monster, has about 8 times 10 to the 53rd power elements.
tossups.r: The six ways to rotate or flip an equilateral triangle form the smallest non-commutative one. For 10 points, name these algebraic structures.

tossups.p: Two of these structures are called isomorphic if they have exactly the same pattern of combining, even when their elements look completely different, like the four rotations of a square and the numbers 0 through 3 added on a 4-hour clock.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these algebraic structures, each a set with an operation that obeys closure, associativity, identity, and inverses.

tossups.p: The whole numbers 0, 1, 2, 3, and so on do not form one of these under addition, because 1 has no inverse among them, but the integers do, since adding negative 1 undoes adding 1. The nonzero integers under multiplication fail too, because 2 has no integer inverse.
tossups.r: Évariste Galois named them. For 10 points, name these algebraic structures, whose rules include closure, associativity, an identity, and inverses.

tossups.p: Burnside’s lemma uses these structures to count how many different necklaces can be made from colored beads when turning a necklace around does not count as making a new one. William Burnside also wrote an early major textbook on these structures in 1897.
tossups.r: In 2010, computers showed that every position of a Rubik’s Cube, whose moves form one of these, can be solved in 20 moves or fewer. For 10 points, name these algebraic structures.

Repeating 3-D crystal patterns fall into exactly 230 types and flat wallpaper patterns into exactly 17, each type being one of these
Chemists label molecular shapes with them (water is C2v, methane is Td) and use character tables to predict which vibrations absorb infrared light
Ludwig Sylow’s theorems (1872) describe the pieces with prime-power sizes inside finite ones
Cauchy’s theorem: if a prime p divides a finite one’s size, it has an element that first returns to the identity after exactly p steps

trap.title: Which “theory” is it?
trap.body: Group theory, set theory, and graph theory sound alike. Group theory is about combining moves, like Rubik’s Cube turns or the rotations and flips of a shape, under four rules. Set theory is about collections and sizes of infinity, and graph theory is about dots joined by lines, like Euler’s seven bridges. And a tossup about Évariste Galois’s life, such as his duel, wants the man himself, not the structures he named.
trap.fix: Listen for the four rules (closure, associativity, identity, inverses), “abelian,” symmetry, the Rubik’s Cube, or the Monster: that means groups. Venn diagrams, Cantor, and infinity mean sets; vertices, edges, and Königsberg mean graphs. If all you know is “the math of symmetry,” say “group theory,” because “symmetry” alone only earns a prompt.
trap.line: Real answer line: groups (or group theory; prompt on abstract algebra or symmetry)

topics.name: Set theory
topics.kicker: The math of collections · Venn diagrams and sizes of infinity
topics.briefing: Set theory is the math of collections, called sets, such as the counting numbers, the letters of the alphabet, or the players on a Quiz Bowl team; Venn diagrams use overlapping circles to show which members two sets share. In the 1870s, Georg Cantor used sets to make a startling discovery: some infinities are bigger than others, so there are more real numbers than counting numbers. Set theory became the foundation on which almost all of modern math is built.

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: André Weil [“VAY”] chose the symbol for the empty example of these collections in 1939, borrowing the slashed letter Ø from the Norwegian alphabet. That empty one counts as a part of every such collection, and a collection with n members has 2 to the n sub-collections in all.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these collections of objects, which are written with curly braces and drawn as overlapping circles in Venn diagrams.

tossups.p: Giuseppe Peano [“pay-AH-noh”] introduced a symbol based on the Greek letter epsilon in 1889 to mean “is a member of” one of these collections. The number of members of one of these is called its cardinality, and the one with no members at all is called empty.
tossups.r: The union of two of these joins their members, while their intersection keeps only shared members. For 10 points, name these collections.

tossups.p: Ernst Zermelo [“tsair-MAY-loh”] published axioms for this branch of math in 1908, and Abraham Fraenkel [“FRENG-kul”] later improved them; with the axiom of choice added, the system is called ZFC. Mathematicians treat ZFC as the foundation on which nearly all of mathematics can be built.
tossups.r: Georg Cantor founded this branch of math, which uses Venn diagrams to picture collections. For 10 points, name this field that studies collections of objects.

tossups.p: Using the axiom of choice, Stefan Banach [“BAH-nahk”] and Alfred Tarski proved in 1924 that a solid ball can be cut into finitely many pieces and reassembled into two balls, each the same size as the original. That axiom says you can always pick a member from each of any number of nonempty collections.
tossups.r: Venn diagrams picture its unions and intersections. For 10 points, name this branch of math that studies collections of objects, founded by Georg Cantor.

tossups.p: Kurt Gödel [“GUR-dul”] showed in 1940 that the continuum hypothesis cannot be disproved from the standard axioms of this field, and Paul Cohen invented a method called forcing to show in 1963 that it cannot be proved either. Cohen won a Fields Medal in 1966 for that work.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this branch of math, founded by Georg Cantor, that studies collections and shows some infinities are bigger than others.

tossups.p: In 1902, Bertrand Russell sent Gottlob Frege [“FRAY-guh”] a letter about a paradox just as the second volume of Frege’s _Basic Laws of Arithmetic_ was going to press. That paradox asks whether the collection of all collections that are not members of themselves is a member of itself.
tossups.r: A popular version imagines a barber who shaves exactly the men who don’t shave themselves. For 10 points, name this branch of math, pictured with Venn diagrams.

tossups.p: Leopold Kronecker [“KROH-neck-er”] fiercely opposed the founder of this field, but David Hilbert declared that no one would expel mathematicians from the “paradise” that founder had created. In this field, two collections have the same size if their members can be paired off one-to-one.
tossups.r: That founder, Georg Cantor, showed that some infinities are bigger than others. For 10 points, name this branch of math that studies collections.

tossups.p: In his 1638 book _Two New Sciences_, Galileo noticed that the perfect squares 1, 4, 9, 16, and so on can be paired with all the counting numbers, even though most counting numbers are not squares. This field later defined two infinite collections to be the same size whenever such a pairing exists.
tossups.r: Georg Cantor founded this field in the 1870s. For 10 points, name this branch of math, which pictures collections with Venn diagrams.

tossups.p: Removing the middle third of a line segment, then the middle thirds of the pieces that remain, and so on forever, leaves a fractal “dust” that has zero total length but still contains uncountably many points. That fractal is named for the founder of this branch of math.
tossups.r: That founder was Georg Cantor. For 10 points, name this branch of math whose Venn diagrams show unions and intersections of collections.

tossups.p: John von Neumann [“NOY-mahn”] built the whole numbers out of nothing: 0 is the empty collection, 1 is the collection containing 0, 2 is the collection containing 0 and 1, and so on. In this field, the size of a collection is called its cardinality.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this branch of math, founded by Georg Cantor, that studies collections such as {1, 2, 3}, which has 8 sub-collections.

tossups.p: Ernst Schröder [“SHRUR-der”] and Felix Bernstein name a theorem saying that if each of two collections can be matched one-to-one with part of the other, then the two collections are the same size. In this field, the counting numbers, the integers, and the fractions all turn out to be the same size.
tossups.r: Its union and intersection operations combine collections. For 10 points, name this branch of math, founded by Georg Cantor, that uses Venn diagrams.

tossups.p: After proving in 1877 that a square contains no more points than a line segment, this field’s founder wrote to Richard Dedekind [“DAY-duh-kint”], “I see it, but I don’t believe it!” That founder also used a diagonal argument to show that the real numbers can never be fully listed.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this branch of math founded by Georg Cantor, which studies collections drawn in Venn diagrams.

tossups.p: In Hilbert’s Hotel, which has infinitely many rooms and no vacancies, a new guest can still get a room if every guest moves from room n to room n plus 1. That thought experiment shows that an infinite collection can be matched one-to-one with a part of itself.
tossups.r: John Venn’s overlapping-circle diagrams, introduced in 1880, picture its collections. For 10 points, name this branch of math, founded by Georg Cantor.

tossups.p: A diagonal argument shows that any list of real numbers must leave some out, by building a new number that differs from the first number in its first digit, from the second in its second digit, and so on. The size of the counting numbers is written aleph-null, using the first letter of the Hebrew alphabet.
tossups.r: Georg Cantor used these ideas to show some infinities are bigger than others. For 10 points, name this branch of math.

tossups.p: The axiom of extensionality says that two of these collections are equal exactly when they have the same members, so the collection containing 1 and 2 is the same as the collection containing 2, 1, and 1 again. Order and repetition do not matter in these collections.
tossups.r: De Morgan’s laws connect their unions, intersections, and complements. For 10 points, name these collections, often drawn as circles in Venn diagrams.

clues.t: Studies collections of distinct objects, called elements or members, written in curly braces like {1, 2, 3}
Venn diagrams use overlapping circles to show which members two of these collections share
Founded by Georg Cantor in the 1870s, who showed that some infinities are bigger than others
The union (∪) of two of them joins all their members; the intersection (∩) keeps only the shared members
The empty one has no members and is written ∅ or {}; it counts as a part of every collection
The number of members of one of them is called its cardinality
A collection with n members has 2^n sub-collections ({1, 2, 3} has 8); Cantor proved the collection of all sub-collections is always bigger than the original
Two collections are the same size if their members pair off one-to-one; the counting numbers, integers, and fractions are all the same size (countably infinite)
Cantor’s diagonal argument (1891) proved that no list can include every real number, so the real numbers are uncountable
The size of the counting numbers is called aleph-null (ℵ₀), after the first letter of the Hebrew alphabet
Russell’s paradox: does the collection of all collections that are not members of themselves contain itself? The barber who shaves exactly the men who don’t shave themselves is a version
De Morgan’s laws: outside a union is the overlap of the two outsides, and outside an intersection is the union of the two outsides
John Venn introduced his overlapping-circle diagrams in 1880; Leonhard Euler had drawn similar circle diagrams for logic long before
André Weil chose the symbol ∅ for the empty one in 1939, borrowing the letter Ø from the Norwegian alphabet
Giuseppe Peano introduced a symbol based on the Greek epsilon (now ∈) in 1889 to mean “is a member of”
Ernst Zermelo’s 1908 axioms, improved by Abraham Fraenkel, plus the axiom of choice form ZFC, the standard foundation of math
Banach–Tarski paradox (1924): with the axiom of choice, a ball can be cut into finitely many pieces and rebuilt into two balls of the original size
The continuum hypothesis (Hilbert’s first problem) can’t be disproved (Gödel, 1940) or proved (Paul Cohen’s forcing, 1963) from the usual axioms; Cohen won a 1966 Fields Medal
Russell’s 1902 letter about his paradox reached Gottlob Frege just as volume 2 of Frege’s _Basic Laws of Arithmetic_ was going to press
Leopold Kronecker fiercely opposed Cantor; David Hilbert defended him: “No one shall expel us from the paradise that Cantor has created”
Galileo’s paradox (_Two New Sciences_, 1638): the perfect squares can be paired with all the counting numbers
Cantor’s middle-thirds fractal: keep removing middle thirds of a segment to get a “dust” with zero length but uncountably many points
John von Neumann built the whole numbers from the empty collection: 0 = {}, 1 = {0}, 2 = {0, 1}, and so on
Schröder–Bernstein theorem: if each of two collections matches one-to-one with part of the other, they are the same size
After proving (1877) that a square has no more points than a line segment, Cantor wrote to Richard Dedekind, “I see it, but I don’t believe it!”
Hilbert’s Hotel: a full hotel with infinitely many rooms still fits a new guest, since an infinite collection can match one-to-one with part of itself
Axiom of extensionality: two collections are equal exactly when they have the same members, so order and repetition don’t matter

trap.title: Field, founder, or diagram?
trap.body: Set theory tossups lean on Georg Cantor, Venn diagrams, and infinity, and each of those is also its own answer line. If the question asks for “this branch of math” or “these collections,” saying “Cantor” or “Venn diagrams” loses the tossup, and so does a too-specific answer like “empty set” or “power set.” Questions about logic can also bring up Russell’s paradox, so listen for what is being asked.
trap.fix: Listen for the noun: “this branch of math,” “this field,” or “these collections” means set theory (or sets). “This man” means Cantor or Venn, and “this concept” may mean infinity. Singular “set” and plural “sets” are both fine.
trap.line: Real answer line: set theory (accept sets; prompt on logic or mathematical logic)

topics.name: Integers
topics.kicker: Whole numbers, their negatives, and zero · Symbol ℤ, for German _Zahlen_
topics.dates: Rules for negatives and zero: Brahmagupta, 628 CE
topics.briefing: The integers are the whole numbers together with their negatives: …, −3, −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, 3, …, stretching forever in both directions along the number line. They have no fractions or decimals, so 7 and −12 are integers but ½ is not; mathematicians write the integers as ℤ, from the German word _Zahlen_, meaning “numbers.” Adding, subtracting, or multiplying two integers always gives another integer, but dividing them often doesn’t.
topics.answerHtml: integers (prompt on Z or whole numbers; do not accept “natural numbers”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In 2014, YouTube’s view counter for the “Gangnam Style” music video passed 2,147,483,647, the largest value a signed 32-bit computer variable for these numbers can hold, so YouTube switched to 64 bits. Such a variable can store values from negative 2,147,483,648 up to that maximum.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these numbers, such as negative 3, 0, and 7, which include the whole numbers and their negatives.

tossups.p: Many computers count time as seconds since January 1, 1970, stored as a signed 32-bit number of this type, a count that runs out of room on January 19, 2038. A similar overflow happens whenever a calculation produces one of these numbers too big for the space reserved for it.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these numbers, which have no fractional or decimal part and can be positive, negative, or zero.

tossups.p: Equations named for Diophantus [“dy-oh-FAN-tus”] of Alexandria ask only for solutions that are these numbers. Hilbert’s tenth problem asked for a method to decide whether any such equation has solutions, and in 1970 Yuri Matiyasevich [“mah-tee-yah-SEH-vich”] completed a proof that no such method exists.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these numbers, symbolized by a double-struck capital Z from the German word _Zahlen_, which include negative 5, 0, and 12.

tossups.p: In 1994, Andrew Wiles completed his proof that the equation a to the n plus b to the n equals c to the n has no solutions in positive numbers of this kind when n is greater than 2. Pierre de Fermat had claimed a proof of that fact in a book margin around 1637.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these numbers that sit evenly spaced along the number line, including zero and the negatives of the counting numbers.

tossups.p: Carl Friedrich Gauss studied complex numbers a plus b i in which a and b are both of this type, numbers that are named for him. The Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic says that each of these numbers greater than 1 factors into primes in exactly one way.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these numbers, such as negative 4, which are closed under addition, subtraction, and multiplication but not division.

tossups.p: These numbers form a ring rather than a field, because under multiplication only 1 and negative 1 have inverses among them; those two are called the units. Under addition, however, every one of them has an inverse, its opposite, so they form a commutative group.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these numbers, such as negative 9, 0, and 4, that are written with a double-struck Z.

tossups.p: The division algorithm says that dividing one of these numbers by a positive one always leaves a unique remainder that is at least 0 but smaller than the divisor; for example, 17 divided by 5 gives 3 with remainder 2. Negative 17 divided by 5 gives negative 4 with remainder 3.
tossups.r: Adding, subtracting, or multiplying two of them always gives another. For 10 points, name these numbers, the whole numbers together with their negatives.

tossups.p: Étienne Bézout’s [“bay-ZOOZ”] identity says that the greatest common divisor of two of these numbers can be written as a sum of multiples of them, as when 2, the greatest common divisor of 10 and 6, equals 10 times 2 minus 6 times 3. Euclid’s algorithm finds that divisor by repeated division.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these numbers, symbolized by a double-struck Z, which include 0 and the negatives of the counting numbers.

tossups.p: Pick’s theorem, published by Georg Pick in 1899, finds the area of a polygon whose corners sit on points whose coordinates are both these numbers: count the grid points inside, add half the grid points on the edges, and subtract 1.
tossups.r: Such points are called lattice points. For 10 points, name these numbers, which label the evenly spaced marks on a number line in both directions from 0.

tossups.p: Srinivasa Ramanujan [“rah-MAH-nuh-jun”] studied partitions, the ways to write a positive number of this type as a sum of positive ones, such as 2 plus 2 and 3 plus 1 for 4. He noticed that the numbers of partitions of 4, 9, 14, 19, and so on are always multiples of 5.
tossups.r: No fractions are allowed among them. For 10 points, name these numbers, which include all the whole numbers and their negatives.

tossups.p: The Babylonian clay tablet Plimpton 322, written around 1800 BCE, records numbers from Pythagorean triples, which are positive numbers of this type a, b, and c with a squared plus b squared equal to c squared. The simplest such triple is 3, 4, and 5.
tossups.r: In 628 CE, Brahmagupta [“brah-muh-GOOP-tuh”] wrote rules for arithmetic with positives, negatives, and zero. For 10 points, name these numbers, which include negative 2, 0, and 5 but not one-half.

tossups.p: In his 1801 book _Disquisitiones Arithmeticae_ [“dis-kwiz-ih-tee-OH-nays ar-ith-MET-ih-kye”], Carl Friedrich Gauss introduced the triple-bar symbol for congruence, writing that two of these numbers are congruent if they leave the same remainder when divided by some number. That idea is often called clock arithmetic.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these numbers, such as negative 8, 0, and 3, which can be positive, negative, or zero.

tossups.p: The name of these numbers comes from a Latin word meaning “whole” or “untouched.” Leopold Kronecker [“KROH-neck-er”] reportedly said that God made these numbers and that “all else is the work of man,” and Stephen Hawking edited a 2005 collection of math classics whose title comes from that remark.
tossups.r: They have no fractional parts. For 10 points, name these numbers, which include zero, the counting numbers, and their negatives.

tossups.p: Kenneth Iverson named the floor and ceiling operations in 1962; they round any real number down or up to the nearest of these numbers, so the floor of negative 2.5 is negative 3. Every one of these numbers is either even or odd, and 0 counts as even.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these numbers, the whole numbers together with their negatives, which are written with a double-struck Z.

tossups.p: There are exactly as many of these numbers as there are counting numbers, since they can be listed 0, 1, negative 1, 2, negative 2, and so on. Ratios of two of these numbers, with a bottom that is not 0, are called rational numbers.
tossups.r: Every one of them has an opposite, like 7 and negative 7, that adds with it to 0. For 10 points, name these numbers.

clues.t: The whole numbers and their negatives: …, −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, …, with no fractions or decimals
Written with a double-struck ℤ, from the German word _Zahlen_ (“numbers”)
The evenly spaced marks on a number line, stretching forever in both directions from 0
Adding, subtracting, or multiplying two of them always gives another one, but dividing often does not
0 is one of them, neither positive nor negative; every one is even or odd, and 0 counts as even
Every one has an opposite (additive inverse) that adds with it to 0, like 7 and −7
Rational numbers are ratios of two of them, with a bottom that is not 0
There are exactly as many of them as counting numbers: list them 0, 1, −1, 2, −2, and so on
Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic: each one greater than 1 factors into primes in exactly one way
Brahmagupta (628 CE) wrote rules for arithmetic with positive numbers (“fortunes”), negative numbers (“debts”), and zero
Leopold Kronecker reportedly said God made them and “all else is the work of man”; Stephen Hawking’s 2005 anthology takes its title from it
Floor and ceiling (named by Kenneth Iverson, 1962) round a real number down or up to one of them: the floor of −2.5 is −3
A signed 32-bit one ranges from −2,147,483,648 to 2,147,483,647; in 2014 the “Gangnam Style” view count outgrew it, so YouTube switched to 64 bits
Year 2038 problem: clocks that store seconds since January 1, 1970, as a signed 32-bit one run out of room on January 19, 2038
Diophantine equations, named for Diophantus of Alexandria, ask only for solutions of this kind
Hilbert’s tenth problem asked for a method to decide whether such equations have solutions; Yuri Matiyasevich completed the proof that none exists (1970)
Fermat’s Last Theorem: aⁿ + bⁿ = cⁿ has no positive solutions of this kind for n > 2; claimed c. 1637, proved by Andrew Wiles (1994)
Complex numbers a + bi with a and b both of this kind are named for Carl Friedrich Gauss
They form a ring, not a field: under multiplication only 1 and −1 (the units) have inverses; under addition they form a commutative group
Division algorithm: dividing by a positive one leaves a unique remainder that is at least 0 and less than the divisor: 17 ÷ 5 is 3 R 2, and −17 ÷ 5 is −4 R 3
Bézout’s identity: the greatest common divisor of two of them is a sum of their multiples, like 2 = 10 × 2 − 6 × 3
Pick’s theorem (Georg Pick, 1899): a polygon with corners on lattice points has area = inside points + half the edge points − 1
Ramanujan studied partitions (ways to write a number as a sum of positive ones) and saw that the counts for 4, 9, 14, 19, … are always multiples of 5
The Babylonian tablet Plimpton 322 (c. 1800 BCE) records numbers from Pythagorean triples, like 3, 4, 5
Gauss introduced the ≡ sign for congruence (same remainder, “clock arithmetic”) in _Disquisitiones Arithmeticae_ (1801)
Their name comes from a Latin word meaning “whole” or “untouched”

trap.title: Integers or whole numbers?
trap.body: In many U.S. classrooms, “whole numbers” means 0, 1, 2, 3, … with no negatives, while the integers also include −1, −2, −3, …. The natural numbers or counting numbers (1, 2, 3, …) are a smaller collection still, and the rational numbers are a bigger one that adds fractions. Saying “whole numbers” or just the letter “Z” only earns a prompt, “natural numbers” is wrong, and so is the calculus sound-alike “integrals.”
trap.fix: If the clues mention negatives, zero, opposites, or the symbol ℤ, say “integers.” If they add fractions or ratios, the answer may be rational numbers; if only 1, 2, 3, …, it may be natural numbers. Integrals are areas under curves, a different answer line.
trap.line: Real answer line: integers (prompt on Z or whole numbers; do not accept “natural numbers”)

topics.name: Functions (math)
topics.kicker: Rules that turn each input into exactly one output · Written f(x)
topics.briefing: A function is a rule that takes each input and gives back exactly one output, like a machine that doubles any number you feed it. We write f(x) = 2x, so f(3) = 6, a notation first written by Leonhard Euler. Functions can be drawn as graphs, and a graph shows a function only if no vertical line crosses it more than once; almost every formula in science, from a ball’s height over time to a pizza’s price by size, is a function.
topics.answerHtml: functions (accept maps or mappings; prompt on relations; do not accept a specific kind like “trigonometric functions”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Peter Gustav Lejeune Dirichlet [“deer-ih-KLAY”], often credited with the modern definition of these objects, described an example that equals 1 at every rational number and 0 at every irrational number. That example is not continuous at any point, since every interval contains both kinds of numbers.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these mathematical rules, written f of x, that assign each input exactly one output.

tossups.p: In 1872, Karl Weierstrass [“VY-er-shtrahss”] surprised mathematicians with an example of these objects that is continuous everywhere but has a slope, or derivative, nowhere; its graph is jagged at every scale, like a fractal. Its formula adds up infinitely many cosine waves.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these rules that give exactly one output for each input, which pass the vertical line test.

tossups.p: In the 1930s, Alonzo Church built his lambda calculus, a system that expresses all computation using only these objects, which can even take other examples of these objects as inputs. Programming languages such as Lisp and Haskell borrowed ideas from that system.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these rules, written with notation like f of x, whose allowed inputs form a domain and whose outputs form a range.

tossups.p: Luitzen Brouwer’s [“BROW-erz”] fixed-point theorem says that any continuous example of these objects that sends a disk into itself must leave at least one point exactly where it started, which is why gently stirring a cup of coffee always leaves some point of the surface where it began.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these mathematical rules, often written f of x, that assign exactly one output to every input.

tossups.p: Tibor Radó [“RAH-doh”] defined the “busy beaver” example of these objects in 1962, and no computer program can calculate all of its values, because it grows faster than any computable example. Alan Turing’s 1936 paper on computable numbers introduced the machines used to decide which of these can be computed.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these rules that give each input exactly one output, which are tested on graphs with a vertical line.

tossups.p: In 1718, Johann Bernoulli [“ber-NOO-lee”] defined one of these as a quantity built in any way from a variable and constants. Gottfried Leibniz [“LYBE-nits”] had first used their name in 1673, for quantities connected to points on a curve, such as its slope.
tossups.r: Leonhard Euler was the first to write them as f of x. For 10 points, name these rules that assign each input exactly one output.

tossups.p: Brook Taylor’s 1715 book showed how to write a smooth example of these objects as an infinite sum of powers of x, built from its derivatives at a single point. Colin Maclaurin later popularized the special case centered at 0.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these rules that assign exactly one output to each input, whose graphs pass the vertical line test.

tossups.p: Joseph Fourier’s [“FOOR-ee-ayz”] 1822 book on the flow of heat claimed that these objects could be written as infinite sums of sine and cosine waves, an idea at the heart of modern signal processing. A continuous example of these objects can be graphed without lifting your pencil.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these rules, written f of x, that give exactly one output for each input.

tossups.p: Leonhard Euler’s gamma example of these objects extends the factorial to fractions, so that its value at one-half equals the square root of pi. Unlike the factorial, which only accepts whole numbers, gamma accepts any positive real number as an input.
tossups.r: Its allowed inputs are called its domain. For 10 points, name these rules that assign each input exactly one output.

tossups.p: One of these objects is called a bijection if it is both one-to-one and onto, pairing up the members of two collections perfectly; Georg Cantor used such pairings to compare sizes of infinity. One of these passes the horizontal line test exactly when it is one-to-one.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these rules, often written f of x, whose graphs pass the vertical line test.

tossups.p: In 1890, Giuseppe Peano [“pay-AH-noh”] described a continuous example of these objects whose outputs fill an entire square, even though its inputs come from a single line segment. David Hilbert described a similar space-filling curve in 1891. Peano’s curve must pass through some points of the square more than once.
tossups.r: In set theory, one of these is a collection of ordered pairs in which no first coordinate repeats. For 10 points, name these rules that give each input exactly one output.

tossups.p: Augustin-Louis Cauchy [“koh-SHEE”] studied the equation saying that the output for the sum of two inputs always equals the sum of their two outputs; its only continuous solutions are straight lines through the origin. The linear examples of these objects, such as y equals 3x plus 2, graph as straight lines.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these rules, often written f of x, that assign exactly one output to each input.

tossups.p: Oliver Heaviside names a step-shaped example of these objects that outputs 0 for every negative input and 1 for every positive input. Pierre-François Verhulst [“vair-HULST”] used an S-shaped “logistic” example to model how a population grows quickly at first and then levels off.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these rules, written f of x, whose inputs form a domain and whose outputs form a range.

tossups.p: Leonhard Euler’s 1748 textbook _Introductio in analysin infinitorum_ made these objects the central idea of calculus. Composing two of these means feeding the output of the first into the second, and an inverse undoes the original, so its graph is the original graph reflected over the line y equals x.
tossups.r: Euler was the first to write them as f of x. For 10 points, name these rules that assign each input exactly one output.

tossups.p: Even examples of these objects, such as x squared, have graphs that are mirror images across the y-axis, while odd examples, such as x cubed, look the same after a half-turn around the origin. Only one-to-one examples, which pass the horizontal line test, have inverses.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these rules, written f of x, that give exactly one output for each input.

clues.t: A rule that assigns each input exactly one output
Written f(x), read “f of x”: if f(x) = 2x, then f(3) = 6
Vertical line test: a graph shows one of these only if no vertical line crosses it more than once
Its allowed inputs make up the domain, and its outputs make up the range
Leonhard Euler was the first to write f(x), and his 1748 _Introductio in analysin infinitorum_ made them the central idea of calculus
Gottfried Leibniz first used their name in 1673, for quantities tied to points on a curve, such as its slope
Composition, written f(g(x)), feeds the output of g into f
An inverse undoes the original; its graph is the original’s reflection across the line y = x
Horizontal line test: it is one-to-one, and so has an inverse, if no horizontal line crosses its graph twice
Even ones (like x²) mirror across the y-axis; odd ones (like x³) look the same after a half-turn around the origin
Linear ones, y = mx + b, graph as straight lines with slope m
A continuous one can be graphed without lifting your pencil
In set theory, one is a collection of ordered pairs in which no first coordinate repeats
Dirichlet, often credited with the modern definition, described one equal to 1 at rationals and 0 at irrationals, continuous nowhere
Karl Weierstrass (1872) found one that is continuous everywhere but has a slope nowhere, built from infinitely many cosine waves
Alonzo Church’s lambda calculus (1930s) expresses all computation using only these; Lisp and Haskell borrowed ideas from it
Brouwer’s fixed-point theorem: a continuous one sending a disk into itself leaves some point in place, like gently stirred coffee
Tibor Radó’s busy beaver (1962) grows faster than any computable one, so no program can find all its values
Johann Bernoulli (1718) defined one as a quantity built in any way from a variable and constants
Brook Taylor’s 1715 book wrote smooth ones as infinite sums of powers of x; Colin Maclaurin popularized the case centered at 0
Joseph Fourier’s 1822 book on heat wrote them as infinite sums of sine and cosine waves
Euler’s gamma extends the factorial to fractions; its value at 1/2 is √π
A bijection is both one-to-one and onto, pairing two collections perfectly; Georg Cantor used such pairings to compare infinities
Giuseppe Peano’s 1890 space-filling curve is a continuous one whose outputs fill a whole square; David Hilbert gave another in 1891
Cauchy’s equation: the output for a sum of inputs equals the sum of their outputs; its continuous solutions are lines through the origin
Oliver Heaviside’s step one is 0 for negative inputs and 1 for positive ones; Verhulst’s S-shaped logistic one models population growth

trap.title: General idea or one kind?
trap.body: Tossups on this answer line describe the general idea: a rule that gives each input exactly one output. Other tossups want one kind, like trigonometric functions, polynomials, or logarithms, and giving a specific kind here, or the general word there, loses the tossup. Saying “relation” earns only a prompt (every function is a relation, but not every relation is a function), and “domain” or “range” names just one part.
trap.fix: If the clues jump between many kinds (Dirichlet’s and Weierstrass’s strange examples, the vertical line test, f(x), domain and range), say “functions.” If every clue is about sine and cosine, or about one formula family, name that family instead.
trap.line: Real answer line: functions (accept maps or mappings; prompt on relations; do not accept a specific kind like “trigonometric functions”)
